definitions.R0: least R > 0 with R = -p (mod 4q) (selected_residual); R0 = 3 (mod 4) and q | a = (p+R0)/4
definitions.class_modulus_M: 840 * prod(primes 11 <= ell <= q); the class c = p mod M fixes q, R0 and p mod ell for all ell <= q
definitions.forced: prime ell <= q divides a for EVERY p in the class c mod M; equivalently p = -R0 (mod ell) for odd ell, p = -R0 (mod 8) for ell = 2. Primes ell > q are never forced.
definitions.r1_candidates: ALL prime factors r1 of R0 with r1 = 3 (mod 4); admissibility is the existential over them
definitions.A1: (q|r1) = +1  [= the ell = q instance of (A2), since q | a always]
definitions.A2: (ell|r1) = +1 for every forced odd ell <= q (q included); a forced ell = r1 counts as a violation, (r1|r1) = 0
definitions.A3_as_printed: r1 = 3 (mod 8) with a odd, or r1 = 7 (mod 8) with a even
definitions.two_adic_ok: the ell = 2 instance of (A2): (2|r1) = +1 whenever 2 | a, i.e. r1 = 7 (mod 8) whenever a is even. Weaker than A3_as_printed: it also admits the 'mixed' case r1 = 7 (mod 8) with a odd.
definitions.nonempty_family: A1 and A2 and two_adic_ok - the exact condition for {p = c (mod M) : every prime factor of a is a QR mod r1} to be nonempty, since a violation at a forced ell puts that ell in every member's factorization
definitions.case_split: 2-adic configuration of the selected r1: A (r1 = 3 mod 8, a odd) / B (r1 = 7 mod 8, a even) / mixed (r1 = 7 mod 8, a odd) / excluded (r1 = 3 mod 8, a even, family empty)
definitions.counting_unit: one hard prime = one first rung; primes sharing a class mod M give identical verdicts, so shares are shares of first rungs exactly as in Remark 5.9

notes: (A3) as PRINTED (case A or case B only) is satisfied by 5 first rungs, not 9: the quoted headline count includes the 'mixed' configuration r1 = 7 (mod 8) with a odd, which is 2-adically admissible (2 does not divide a, so ell = 2 imposes no condition) but is not one of the two cases (A3) lists. The quoted case split names those 4 mixed rungs explicitly, so the headline count is the nonempty-family count reported here.

The quoted 'R0 is prime for 93.4% of hard primes' does NOT match: R0 is prime for 25,700 of 39,391 first rungs = 65.2%. 93.4% is exactly 100% - 6.6% = the share of first rungs with NO r1 passing (A1) (36,798/39,391 = 93.4%). Prime R0 is a strict subset of that: prime R0 always fails (A1) (its only prime factor is r1 = R0, and Theorem J gives (q|R0) = (p|q) = -1), but composite R0 can fail (A1) too.
